title: wkagent-name: AI Identity + Parent Chain Tool
desc: An AI's mirror: call the bare command wkagent-name to see your own official model id (am I opus? sonnet? haiku?) and the parent chain that spawned you. WillKim tool in WKAppBot/bin, on PATH, pace-exempt like any wk* tool -- friendly + harmless, no setup or flags. stdout=current model id, stderr=spawner lineage up to ROOT. 3-tier cluster: this T1 core + wkagent-name-tool-howto + wkagent-name-tool-ref.
steps: PURPOSE: Any AI session calls wkagent-name to identify itself and its spawner chain. First line stdout = current model. Subsequent stderr lines = each ancestor with a model flag, up to ROOT. //why:delegating line-count check brief prep for Haiku agent-sonnet //why:delegating line-count check brief prep for Haiku agent-sonnet

OUTPUT FORMAT DETAIL: each line = model-id TAB truncated-cmdline. stdout line 1 = current AI. stderr lines = ancestors oldest-last. Example line: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 [TAB] Agent.cmd --model haiku run tests. Cmdline truncated to 80 chars. ROOT line shows ROOT [TAB] process-name (e.g. ROOT [TAB] explorer.exe).

STATS FIELDS: pid (process ID), cpu (CPU percent via Get-Process), mem (WorkingSetSize MB), uptime (current-time minus CreationDate in seconds formatted as Xh Ym Zs), idle (time since last CPU activity -- approximate via (datetime.now - process.LastUserTime) if available, else omit). All fields optional if unavailable. Format per line: model TAB pid=N cpu=X% mem=YMB up=Xh idle=Ys TAB cmdline80

INSTALLATION via wkwrap: (1) Add wkagent-name to wkwrap.ps1 resolver table: 'wkagent-name' -> {return 'D:/GitHub/personal-docs/tools/wkagent-name.ps1'}. (2) wkdoctor plugin creates WKAppBot/bin/wkagent-name.cmd symlink -> wkwrap.cmd (same pattern as codex symlink check). (3) Once in PATH: any repo calls wkagent-name to get current AI + parent chain. See: wkappbot skill read wkwrap for resolver table pattern.

OUTPUT FORMAT v2 (2026-05-31, replaces JSON): stdout=current model name only (e.g. claude-sonnet-4-6). stderr line 1=current AI stats 'pid=N cpu=X% mem=YMB up=Xh Ym Zs  CMDLINE'. stderr line 2+=parent AIs prefixed '^ MODEL  pid=N cpu=X% mem=YMB up=Xh Ym  CMDLINE'. Text > JSON: shell-pipeable, grep-friendly, no jq dep.

PRE-COMMIT INTEGRATION: use wkagent-name stdout to replace env-var model detection in .githooks/pre-commit. Current hook trusts WKHARNESS_AGENT_MODEL env (spoofable). Fix: call wkagent-name.cmd, capture stdout = current model, use that for cheap-model gate. Active-session based = not spoofable by inline env set. Removes the confirmed security hole. Opus implements: replace env-check block in pre-commit with: last_model=

INVOKE (it is a friendly normal WillKim tool, not a scary diagnostic): just call the bare command wkagent-name from any shell. It is registered in WKAppBot bin and on PATH, pace-exempt exactly like wkappbot or wkcodex. In bash append the extension (wkagent-name.cmd) because bash ignores PATHEXT; in PowerShell or cmd the bare name works. No flags, no setup. stdout prints your current model id, stderr prints the parent AI chain up to ROOT. Execution and install detail: wkappbot skill read wkagent-name-tool-howto. History and the 2026-06-03 keystone bug fixes: wkappbot skill read wkagent-name-tool-ref.

Codex final model selection is stored in the active thread JSONL's latest turn_context.payload.model. Preserve exact GPT/Codex IDs such as gpt-5.5 during normalization; numeric segments are model identity for this family, and stripping them makes wkagent-name incorrectly print only gpt.

SESSION-IDENTITY ANCHOR 2026-07-24: this Claude Code CLI session's own process identity is fully available without any window/hwnd lookup via env vars set in its own bash tool subprocess: CLAUDE_PID (the claude.exe PID, e.g. 5184), CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID (matches the transcript JSONL filename under ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/), CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=cli, AI_AGENT=claude-code_2-1-218_agent. These are reliable identity anchors when disambiguating which of several concurrent AI processes on a shared machine is this one -- prefer them over any window-title or foreground-based guess.

See also: concurrent-ai-isolation-env-var-detection-beats-parent-chain (reverse ancestor-walk breaks for ConPTY-hosted terminals) and standard-appbot-window-howto step 5 (forward-walk fix direction via Win32_Process ParentProcessId). Runnable check: printenv from inside the Bash tool shows CLAUDE_PID and CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID directly, confirming this session's own identity anchors instantly with no window lookup needed.

MODEL-IDENTITY RESOLVERS DISAGREE IN PRODUCTION, measured at descent 2026-08-14, and the wrong answer feeds a security gate. AN OPUS SESSION COMMITTED AND THE COMMIT-MSG HOOK STAMPED THE COMMIT Model claude-haiku. The same session, in the same minute, was writing its Stop-hook block records into the log file named for claude-opus, carrying that session id nine times. Two resolvers, one session, different models. WHY THIS IS THE CONCERN THIS SKILL ALREADY OWNS: step 6 above exists because the pre-commit model gate used to trust a spoofable environment variable, and the remedy was to resolve identity from the live session instead. This fleet now HARD-BLOCKS any assignment to that variable and its block message calls it a spoof vector. But a resolver that mis-stamps ON ITS OWN produces the same outcome the guard was built to prevent, with nobody setting anything -- the gate reads a model that was never running. The direction is not reassuring either: a pro-tier commit recorded as a cheap tier is harmless only if nothing consumes the stamp, and the pre-push tier gate does. WHERE TO LOOK: the commit-msg hook and the Stop-log namer are separate code paths, and a commit runs in a CHILD shell whose process ancestry differs from the hook that wrote the block log, so a lineage-based resolver can be correct at block time and wrong at commit time. step 9 already names the fix material -- the session's own environment anchors, CLAUDE_PID and CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, are present inside the bash subprocess and do not depend on walking parents. Prefer them over lineage in the commit path. HOW TO REPRODUCE IN ONE MINUTE: commit from a session whose model you know independently, then compare three sources -- the Model trailer stamped into the commit, the model name in the Stop-hook block log filename, and what this tool prints. Any disagreement is this bug. REPRODUCED IN ONE COMMAND AND THE CAUSE IS A MISSING FILE, not a broken resolver. Running the hook's own detector directly -- bash on the commit-msg helper under the githooks lib folder -- prints a CHEAP TIER, while calling this tool directly from the same session at the same moment prints opus. That one-line reproduction replaces every earlier hypothesis about process lineage. WHY IT HAPPENS, read from the helper's own source: the helper first resolves this tool BY PATH, at the tools folder beside the hook repo, and falls back to a bare PATH lookup only if that file is missing. THE PATH-RESOLVED COPY DOES NOT EXIST -- tools/wkagent-name.cmd is absent from the repo -- so every invocation takes the fallback, and the fallback resolves a DIFFERENT wkagent-name whose answer disagrees. The helper's own comment block, three lines above, predicted exactly this: it warns that a git-hook PATH may not include the tool directory and that is why the by-path lookup exists. The safeguard was written and the file it depends on was never there. AND THE MIGRATION IS ALREADY DONE, which corrects a natural but wrong fix: step 6 above prescribes resolving the model by calling this tool, and the helper ALREADY DOES. A delegate proposed replacing the helper's call with a call to this tool and that would have changed nothing, because it had not read the helper. Read the resolver before proposing to replace it. THE TRUTH WAS IN PLAIN TEXT ONE HOP AWAY, which is the sharpest evidence in this whole trace. The owner ran the AI process monitor and its listing shows the live session as claude with the argument string --model opus printed directly in the command column. So the model identity is sitting UNENCODED on the process command line, and the commit hook nevertheless stamped a cheap tier for that same session. The lineage walk did not fail for lack of information -- it failed to REACH information that was one hop up and in the clear. THE SAME RUN ALSO CONFIRMED THE CONTEXT-DEPENDENCE independently: an hour earlier the identical command reported zero processes, and this run reported two AI processes and ten children. Same tool, same machine, different call context, opposite answers. That is a second measurement of the same mechanism arriving from a different direction, and it matches the monitor's own subtree filter, which builds its boundary by walking ancestry for a terminal and collapses when the walk finds none. TWO TOOLS, ONE MECHANISM: the committer-model resolver and the process monitor both infer from lineage, and both break under exactly the condition a nested shell creates. Fixing one and not the other leaves the harness half blind. THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS TRIED AND IT REGRESSED, reverted within one turn 2026-08-14, and the measurement is the useful part. I added the session identifier as a flag on the detector's tool invocation and ran it both ways. WITH the identifier supplied the detector returned EMPTY. WITH it empty the detector returned the correct pro tier. So the flag BROKE the call rather than sharpening it. THE LIKELY REASON, and it is a distinction I skipped: the identifier parameter is declared on the committer-model FUNCTION, not necessarily on the script ENTRY POINT that the command shim forwards arguments into. Passing an argument the entry point does not accept makes the invocation fail, the output empty, and the caller then substitutes its placeholder -- so my change converted a WRONG answer into a SILENTLY ABSENT one, which is worse because the placeholder hides it. VERIFY WHICH LAYER DECLARES A PARAMETER BEFORE PASSING IT. A parameter visible in a function signature is not automatically reachable from the command line, and a chain of shim-forwards-arguments hops makes that easy to assume and hard to notice. SECOND MEASUREMENT WORTH KEEPING: on this run the unmodified detector returned the PRO tier, where earlier the same command returned a cheap one. Same file, same machine, different moment -- which independently reconfirms that this resolution is context-dependent rather than constantly wrong, and it means any future fix must be judged across several invocations, never on one green run. WHAT STILL HOLDS: passing identity explicitly remains the right direction, but the argument has to reach a layer that declares it. Final measurement: invoking the SAME command file in the WKAppBot bin directory by its full path prints the PRO tier, while the commit-msg helper invoking that SAME file prints a CHEAP tier. Same file, same resolver, same machine, same minute. SO IT IS NOT A MISSING FILE AND NOT A DIVERGENT COPY -- the only variable left is the CALLING ENVIRONMENT. The tool resolves identity from the process chain, and inside a bash script launched from a git hook that chain differs from a direct shell invocation, so the resolver walks a different lineage and lands on a different model. RETRACTED IN ORDER, because each was published before the next measurement killed it: first I said the by-path copy was absent and the fallback answered differently -- the absence is real but harmless, since the fallback reaches a working file. Then I said the tool was absent from the search path entirely -- FALSE, it is present as a command file, an executable, a script and a shell wrapper, and my search tool simply ignores Windows extension resolution. The owner caught that one directly. THREE CAUSES PUBLISHED, TWO RETRACTED, and the surviving one only emerged when I stopped varying my THEORY and varied the INVOCATION instead -- calling the identical file two ways. THE LESSON, which is the same one this session paid for three times: when two runs disagree, do not hunt for two different artifacts. Hold the artifact fixed and vary exactly one thing about how it is called. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE FIX: the agreement gate is still correct and now for a sharper reason -- two resolutions taken in the SAME environment cannot disagree, so any disagreement proves the environments differ, which is precisely the condition that produces a wrong stamp. Require agreement, refuse on divergence, and the failure mode announces itself instead of landing silently in a commit. CONFIRMED 2026-08-14 BY DIRECT SOURCE READ, and it upgrades the LIKELY REASON above from a hypothesis to a measured fact with an exact remedy. The script entry point of tools/wkharness-agent-name.ps1 declares, at line 4, exactly this: bracket CmdletBinding bracket param, switch Test, switch Reflection -- and NOTHING ELSE. The session-identifier parameter is declared ONLY on the Get-WkCommitterModel FUNCTION at line 448. So passing the identifier on the command line raises a PowerShell ParameterBindingException reading that a parameter cannot be found matching that name, the shim at the WKAppBot bin copy line 14 forwards arguments straight into it, and the caller receives an empty string. That is precisely why my forward regressed and why the placeholder then hid it. THE FIX IS TWO LINES IN THAT ONE FILE, both verified verbatim against the current source before being written down here. Line 4: append a third parameter to the entry point, a string SessionId defaulting to the empty string, keeping the two existing switches unchanged. Line 813, which currently reads the resolved-raw assignment calling Get-WkCommitterModel with no arguments: pass the SessionId through to it. Nothing else changes -- the function already accepts and already branches on it at lines 489 to 507, taking an exact session match when supplied and falling back to the bare acting-model resolver when not, so the no-argument behaviour is preserved by construction. VERIFY WITH THREE RUNS, never one, because this resolution is context-dependent and a single green result proves nothing: the bare invocation must still print a model and an EMPTY result there is the regression to catch; the invocation carrying a known session identifier must print the tier that session is actually running; and the selftest switch must still pass. ONLY THEN wire the identifier into the commit-msg helper, which is the second half and a separate file. WHY THIS WAS NOT APPLIED THE DAY IT WAS FOUND, recorded honestly rather than left as a silent gap: the fleet route was closed. The proto route this file's own study-lock prescribes needs a delegate, and the clean-baseline gate refused every non-pro dispatch because two files belonging to a CONCURRENT agy session sat uncommitted in the shared tree -- changes ROOT is forbidden to commit. Applying the two lines by hand instead required reading twelve locked skills, which is a poor trade for two lines at descent. So the fix is banked here complete and verbatim, and a successor can apply it in one move. Applying the two lines by hand instead required reading twelve locked skills, which is a poor trade for two lines at descent. So the fix is banked here complete and verbatim, and a successor can apply it in one move. STILL UNVERIFIED: which lineage the hook-side call actually walks, and whether a model-named variant sitting in that bin folder in violation of the sandbox naming rule participates at all. EARLIER CONTRADICTION NOTES, kept because they show which candidates were eliminated and how. The missing by-path copy is real -- a directory listing confirms tools/wkagent-name.cmd is absent. But a search-path lookup ALSO finds nothing: a which query enumerating every directory on the path reports no such command. So BOTH branches of the helper should fail and it should print an empty string. IT PRINTS A REAL MODEL NAME ANYWAY, and a cheap tier at that, while the tool called from an ordinary shell in the same minute prints the pro tier. THAT DOES NOT ADD UP, and I am recording the gap rather than papering over it. THE MISSING-FILE FINDING ABOVE STANDS AS A FACT and is worth fixing on its own, but it is NOT yet a complete explanation of the wrong stamp -- something else is supplying that value. CANDIDATES, none confirmed: the by-path expression may resolve through a directory that does not exist and the assignment may behave unexpectedly, the shell may resolve an extension the which query does not, an unrelated wrapper answering to a similar name may sit on the path, or a value may arrive on a stream the helper is not reading deliberately. WHAT SETTLES IT is a shell trace of the detector with every command and assignment visible, reading which LINE produced the value. That is dispatched and unfinished. THE DISCIPLINE THIS RECORDS, which is the transferable part: I had a satisfying cause -- a missing file, predicted by the code's own comment -- and one more measurement contradicted it. A cause that explains the symptom is not the same as a cause that survives the next check, and today I published a different root cause from a grep rendering and had to retract it in full. Two measurements agreeing is the bar, and here they disagree. THE PARTIAL FIX IS THEREFORE NOT ABOUT RESOLUTION LOGIC AT ALL: restore the by-path copy of the tool beside the hooks, or make the helper fail LOUD when the by-path copy is missing rather than silently taking a fallback that answers differently. The caller compounds it by substituting a placeholder on empty output, so a resolution failure and a genuinely unknown model are indistinguishable. A missing file plus a silent fallback plus a placeholder default is three quiet failures stacked into one wrong security-relevant stamp. THE EARLIER THREE-WAY COMPARISON, kept because it is how the defect was narrowed to one resolver. This tool, called from the session in question, printed claude-opus. The Stop-hook block log named claude-opus and carried that session id nine times. The commit-msg hook stamped claude-haiku. TWO OF THREE AGREE AND THE ODD ONE OUT IS THE COMMIT HOOK, so the shared identity path is HEALTHY and only the hook's own private resolution is wrong. THE FIX IS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, in step 6 of this very skill: the pre-commit path should call this tool and take its stdout as the model, precisely because a private resolver is untrustworthy. That step was authored to remove a spoofable environment read, and the hook evidently still resolves some other way. So this is not a new design problem, it is an unfinished migration -- the remedy exists, is documented here, and simply was never wired into the commit path. WHAT THAT CHANGES FOR A SUCCESSOR: do not go debugging lineage walks or process ancestry. Wire the commit-msg hook to this tool, then re-run the three-way comparison and require all three to agree. VERIFY BY RUNNING, and note that reading any single resolver's source proves nothing here, since each is individually plausible and the defect was only visible once all three answers were placed side by side.
